name: Mulberry extract

card.summary: A botanical 'brightener' whose published research is about blood sugar and antioxidants, not skin tone.
card.note: No human skin-brightening trial has been published.

quick.overview:
Mulberry extract comes from Morus trees and is sold in skincare as a plant brightener, with mulberroside F named as the active compound.
The studies found concern other uses, mainly blood glucose and antioxidant chemistry. No human trial of it for skin tone turned up.
quick.mechanism: Cosmetic marketing attributes brightening to mulberroside F. No mechanism in human skin has been documented.
quick.risks: No skin-specific safety data were found. Mulberry fruit and leaf are common food and supplement ingredients.

lead: Mulberry extract is a plant extract from trees of the genus Morus, used in skincare as a botanical brightener aimed at dark spots, uneven tone and melasma. Mulberroside F, a compound from the root, is the constituent usually named as the skin-lightening component, and the fruit and leaves are also sold as dietary supplements.[1][2]

People apply it as a plant-derived alternative to synthetic lighteners, usually in serums or oils intended to even out facial tone. A laboratory study of in vitro mulberry cultures found that mulberroside F content in root and callus extracts correlated with tyrosinase inhibition, the enzyme step in melanin production, and that a crude root extract was not cytotoxic to skin-cell lines.[3]

Human research on topical use is small. A 2011 randomised trial of a 75 percent mulberry extract oil in 50 people with melasma reported improvements in pigmentation scores over eight weeks, and later melasma reviews list mulberry extract oil among agents with less evidence than the best-studied treatments.[4][5][6] Most other published mulberry work concerns blood glucose, antioxidant chemistry and food science.[7][8]

chain: Compound inhibits tyrosinase in laboratory assays
Less melanin production in pigmented areas
angle.text: Mulberry extract is applied topically to fade dark spots and even out facial skin tone. Its proposed route is tyrosinase inhibition by mulberroside F, which would reduce melanin formation in treated areas. A small trial in melasma patients examined a mulberry oil for this purpose.

infobox: Topical brightening ingredient; also food colorant and supplement[1]

paras: Mulberry trees are grown for fruit, for leaves that feed silkworms (especially white mulberry), for bark used in papermaking and for folk medicine.[1] Anthocyanins can be extracted from the fruit and used as natural food colorants, and fruit and leaf products are sold as supplements.[1] The Wikipedia article on mulberry does not discuss skin lightening or mulberroside F.[1]

Mulberroside is described in a 2025 systematic review as one of the main active components of white mulberry root, with reported anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, hypoglycaemic and other pharmacological activities in laboratory and animal work; the same review notes low bioavailability and rapid metabolism.[2]

In cosmetics, mulberry extract is positioned as a plant-derived alternative to synthetic brighteners, with mulberroside F cited by marketers and enthusiasts as the active compound. Products range from root-extract serums to mulberry extract oils of the kind used in the melasma trial.[3][4]

Pigment lightening by mulberry is attributed to inhibition of tyrosinase, the copper enzyme that catalyses early steps of melanin synthesis. In the 2022 in vitro study, mulberroside F content across root and callus extracts correlated positively with tyrosinase-inhibiting activity, and the authors proposed tissue culture as a continuous source of the compound for cosmeceutical use.[3] That work was done in laboratory assays and cell lines rather than in people.[3]

A randomised, single-blind, placebo-controlled trial published in 2011 enrolled 50 patients with melasma, 25 per group, after a repeat open application test to both the mulberry product and the placebo was negative. Participants used a 75 percent Morus alba extract oil or placebo for eight weeks, with visits every four weeks. The mulberry group improved significantly on the Melasma Area and Severity Index (4.076 to 2.884), on Mexameter pigment readings (355.56 to 312.52) and on the MelasQOL quality-of-life score (58.84 to 44.16), while the placebo group improved less on MASI and MelasQOL and showed slightly higher Mexameter readings. Four mulberry-group participants reported mild itching, versus twelve reports of itching or erythema in the placebo group.[4]

Two systematic reviews of topical melasma treatments list mulberry extract among the agents examined. A 2019 review of 35 randomised trials gave strong recommendations to cysteamine, triple combination therapy and tranexamic acid, and a 2022 review described triple combination therapy and hydroquinone as the best-studied agents and mulberry extract oil as having less evidence.[5][6]

Other human studies address different uses. A randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled study reported that an oral mulberry extract improved glucose tolerance and lowered insulin concentrations in adults with normal blood sugar, and several registered trials examine mulberry leaf extract for blood glucose.[7][9][10] Laboratory studies have compared the antioxidant capacity of black and white mulberry extracts in cell models.[8] None of these concerns skin pigmentation.

In the melasma trial, mild itching was the adverse effect reported with the mulberry oil.[4] Mulberry fruit and leaf are common food and supplement ingredients. Other skin-specific safety data on cosmetic mulberry extracts are limited.

timeline.event: Randomised trial of 75% mulberry extract oil for melasma published in the Journal of Drugs in Dermatology.[4]
In vitro study links mulberroside F content in mulberry root extracts to tyrosinase inhibition.[3]
